claims.text: Al0.1CrCoFeNi lies in a low-Al compositional regime that can exhibit a near-single-phase solid solution.
Rapid quenching from the melt produces a baseline with minimal local chemical ordering.
Low-Al AlxCrCoFeNi alloys exhibit chemical clustering or short-range ordering.
Changing Al content or otherwise tuning composition can alter lattice ordering in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni.
A minor compositional adjustment can be selected specifically to enhance local chemical ordering while remaining in the proposed low-Al window.
Slower cooling enhances local chemical ordering relative to rapid cooling in the specified alloy.
Local chemical ordering can influence which microstructural or phase state develops in AlxCrCoFeNi.
Increasing local chemical ordering stabilizes the single-phase solid solution by suppressing intermetallic or dual-phase formation.
Enhanced local ordering lowers free-energy fluctuations and thereby reduces the driving force for unwanted phase transformations.
The more highly ordered variant will decompose more slowly and show a delayed onset of secondary-phase formation.
The more highly ordered variant will retain single-phase stability more effectively during prolonged high-temperature annealing.
Ordering-mediated phase stability preserves high-temperature mechanical strength.
Ordering-mediated phase stability improves oxidation and corrosion resistance.
Ordering-mediated phase stability improves resistance to radiation damage.
Ordering-mediated phase stability maintains or enhances cryogenic toughness.
The baseline alloy has typical phase-instability trends under challenging service conditions.
The hypothesis is bounded to low-Al AlxCrCoFeNi compositions, around x = 0.10, where ordering and a single A1 phase are plausible.
The quantitative relationship between ordering and multi-environment performance retention is uncertain.

contradictions.description: The proposed controlled comparison is described as using identical nominal compositions, but both fields also allow a minor compositional adjustment in the ordered variant. Changing composition would confound the attribution of observed effects specifically to processing-induced ordering.
